reports.text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to report a pattern of cargo fraud and safety violations at the Tessaly Point container terminal, which is run by Orrin Maritime Services. I have tried to raise this internally for almost a year without any result, so I am putting everything I know into this report and I will try to be as precise as I can.

The terminal operations manager, Haldor Brisk, has been instructing crane and yard staff to reclassify refrigerated containers whose temperature recorders show a cold chain break. Instead of flagging them for inspection, the containers are relabeled as dry cargo in the yard system and released to trucks the same day. Most of these containers hold frozen seafood and vaccines bound for regional clinics. When the cold chain is broken on vaccines, there is no way for the clinic to tell by looking at the boxes.

I work the graveyard rotation, four nights on and four off, so I see most of the late releases. My post is the reefer monitoring booth at the end of row K, where the plug-in panels for the refrigerated stacks are. From that booth I can see every alarm come in on the monitor and I log them on a paper sheet as well as on the computer. On a typical week there are between ten and twenty alarms, and lately almost none of them result in an inspection hold.

Mr. Brisk normally leaves the terminal around eight in the evening, but on nights when a large vessel is being worked he stays late in the operations tower and calls the yard planners directly. On those nights the alarm records in the yard system are edited before the morning report is generated. I have compared my paper sheets against the system printout on at least thirty occasions and the alarm entries simply disappear. The edits are made under a shared supervisor login that Haldor Brisk controls.

There is also a safety problem. The straddle carrier drivers are being pushed to exceed the yard speed limit to meet his turnaround targets. Two near misses with pedestrians happened in the last two months, one involving a lashing crew member who was nearly pinned between two stacks. Neither was entered in the incident register. The safety officer, Ingrid Paulsen, was told by Brisk that reporting the near misses would trigger an audit and cost the terminal its insurance discount.

I want to be clear that I am not making this up out of a grudge. I have kept copies of the paper alarm sheets, photographs of the temperature recorder screens, and the printouts showing the edited entries. I can make all of this available to an investigator, and I can explain how the alarm codes work if that helps anyone reading the logs.

I am worried about being identified. I was moved to the reefer booth only after I came back from a long sick leave following a back injury on the quay, and everybody at the terminal knows that story. Before that I was a lasher for six years. I am also the only person on nights who has the reefer technician certificate, so there is nobody else who could have noticed the pattern in the alarm logs. On my days off I am not at the terminal at all, which also narrows it down, because the edits I have documented all happened on nights I was working.

Please handle this carefully.
